source.title: Refusal geometry reflects refusal training: diverse refusal prefixes can raise stable rank and weaken refusal vector ablation attacks

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study estimates a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means refusal vector and applies projection ablation, reporting refusal outcomes on an OLMo model and additional fine-tuned checkpoints. It tests the original intervention in new model and training settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports many stable-rank and gradient measurements. The rows below include textually summarized aggregate geometry results relevant to refusal dimensionality; detailed figure-only per-dataset and per-layer points are not transcribed. Training-target rank results without a reported behavioral outcome are not recorded as separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies the original harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means projection ablation to OLMo-2-0425-1B checkpoints. It reports refusal and harm rates before and after ablation, judged by WildGuard. It also varies refusal-start diversity, both by prompt selection and by controlled fine-tuning, and relates residual stable rank to ablation strength. These results bear on V1, V4, V6 and V7. The method is close to the original but ablates at a single layer and does not test addition or capabilities.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that the low-dimensional refusal direction originates in first-token refusal-training gradients. In their account, repetitive refusal starts concentrate gradients and residuals, which makes single-vector ablation effective. Diversifying refusal starts raises stable rank and reduces ablation deltas, though this is not a complete defense. The study is a single 1B OLMo case study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means vector and projection removal, but evaluates selected layers and prompt sets rather than removing the direction from every layer and position. It additionally studies residual geometry, training gradients, checkpoint comparisons, and refusal-prefix diversity.
record.method_sensitivity: Ablation efficacy varies with checkpoint and layer: the base model has negligible refusal delta, SFT has a smaller delta than later post-base checkpoints, and layers 7–10 are reported as most effective for the Instruct model. Greater refusal-start diversity is associated with weaker ablation. Geometry overlap also varies by layer and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Raw-gradient stable rank amplifies about 2.27× from layer 15 to 7, while gradient-induced updates contract (about 0.83×). Shared-map fits are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-gradient stable rank propagates across layers with bounded transfer factors.

record.problems: Primarily a case study of one small OLMo model family and English-language datasets with relatively small prompt sets. The checkpoint comparison is not causal. Ablation directions are estimated from the same prompt set they attack, an attacker-favorable setting. The reported rank–vulnerability association does not by itself establish causal mediation. Many behavioral values are presented only in figures, and the study does not test general capability preservation, all-layer removal, or added-vector steering.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed figure-only per-dataset and per-layer geometry points in Figures 3, 5–7, 10, 16–17, and 23 are not individually transcribed; aggregate statements reported in the text are recorded in geom_mean7, geom_mean15, geom_overlap15, geom_overlap7, geom_rank7, and geom_rank15. Figure-only fine-tuning rank trajectories and the 8- and 16-start optimization-step curves in Figures 22–23 are also not listed as separate rows because they are not additional matched-checkpoint refusal outcomes; the text reports the Figure 22 maxima in the ft_m8 and ft_m16 notes.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; ablation across all layers and positions; preservation of general capabilities; held-out prompt generalisation (the direction is estimated on the same set it attacks).
Entirely: no weight edit and no released abliterated models.
Entirely: no jailbreak attacks are analysed and no adversarial training against ablation is done.
Multi-direction or cone ablations are explicitly left out of scope; only stable-rank geometry and single-vector weakening are tested.
Cross-language transfer; behavioural transfer of a vector from one checkpoint to another.

missing.what: Per-layer ablation effectiveness for Instruct: the delta is largest at layers 7–10, early layers give almost none, and later layers decline.
Ablation vulnerability over fine-tuning steps: the delta peaks in a narrow window then decays (peak 0.55 at 8 starts, 0.375 at 16 starts).
The leading uncentered singular axis of the gradient updates has mean absolute cosine 0.56 with the refusal direction at layer 7.

record.verdict_notes: V3 was removed from all rows. The ablation is run by the experimenter rather than being a jailbreak, and diverse-prefix SFT is not training against ablation. The geometry mean and overlap rows were moved from V4 to V7. The study is not an original source. Deltas are read only from figure axis ranges.

versions.untested_parts: Tests single-layer difference-in-means projection ablation, not ablation at every layer and position. Does not test adding the direction or whether general capabilities are preserved.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration procedure.

Tests the paper's own difference-in-means ablation attack, not whether other jailbreak attacks suppress this direction. Diverse-prefix fine-tuning weakens ablation but is not training specifically against an ablation attack.

Measures refusal residual and gradient geometry and whether single-vector ablation weakens as residual stable rank increases. Does not compare behavioral effects of ablating multiple principal directions or directly test cone-based interventions.
Does not separate a harmfulness judgment from a refusal decision.

Measures refusal-vector alignment across checkpoints within one OLMo family. Does not test cross-language transfer or apply a vector estimated on one checkpoint to another to measure behavioral transfer.

Tests refusal-start diversity in a controlled fine-tuning setup and descriptively compares released checkpoints. Does not isolate the causal effect of individual released post-training stages; training objectives and data differ.
